kurz: How large the gap between fund return and investor return is, how much of it is due to arithmetic rather than psychology, and what closes it.

bloecke.md:
The return of a fund and the return of its investors are different figures. Both are correct, but they measure different things. The fund return assumes that everything was invested on the first day and stayed invested until the last day. The investor return weights each period by the money that was invested in that period. The difference is called the **behaviour gap**. It is the only quantity in stock market psychology that can be stated in percentage points.

Morningstar measures it every year in its *Mind the Gap* study. In the decade to 31 December 2025, the funds studied returned 9.9% a year, whereas the average invested dollar earned 8.7%. The gap of 1.2 percentage points corresponds to around 12% of the total fund return. In money terms that is about $3.8 trillion, measured against just under $35 trillion that continuous holding would have produced. Kostolany described this process as securities passing from shaky hands into strong hands, and the gap puts a figure on it.

bloecke.formel: 0 = Σ CF(t) / (1 + r)^t     for t = 0 … T
bloecke.erklaerung: The [[investor return]] is the internal rate of return r at which the discounted payments in and out, including the final value, add up to zero. The fund return, by contrast, only chains together the period returns and does not take into account how much money was invested at each point. Both figures are cleanly defined, but can only be compared with caution.

bloecke.md:
## The arithmetical part of the gap

Before interpreting the gap as evidence of human weakness, you have to break it down. Part of it arises purely arithmetically when fluctuating returns coincide with a portfolio that grows over time. With regular contributions, more money is in the market in later years than in early ones. If the weak years come at the end, this lowers the money-weighted return without anyone having made a decision.

bloecke.titel: Effect of the sequence of returns
bloecke.md:
A saver pays in €1,200 at the start of each year. The fund returns +30% in the first year and −10% in the second. Time-weighted, this gives (1.30 × 0.90)^0.5 − 1 = 8.17% a year.

At the end the saver has 1,200 × 1.30 × 0.90 + 1,200 × 0.90 = €2,484. The internal rate of return of this series of payments is 2.32%, so the gap is 5.85 percentage points.

With the sequence reversed, first −10% and then +30%, the fund return stays at exactly 8.17%. The saver now has 1,200 × 0.90 × 1.30 + 1,200 × 1.30 = €2,964 and thus 14.92%. The gap is now plus 6.76 percentage points in the saver's favour.

The behaviour was the same in both cases. The saver made two contributions, bought and sold nothing else and did not act on any market view of their own.

bloecke.titel: Fund and investor return with the sequence reversed
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation in which only the order of the two annual returns is swapped; this changes the investor return by more than twelve percentage points.

bloecke.md:
This is where the academic criticism comes in. In 2026, Fulkerson, Jordan, Riley and Yan argue in the *Financial Analysts Journal* that the damage caused by bad timing is considerably smaller than Morningstar's presentation suggests. Using the same sample as Morningstar's 2025 edition, they put the cost of timing at only about 0.10% a year instead of 1.2 percentage points. What has been established so far is the direction of the effect, but not its size.

Even less robust is the figure that appears most frequently in the sales documents of financial distributors. Since 1994 DALBAR has published the *Quantitative Analysis of Investor Behavior*, whose data go back to 1985, and it used to report gaps of four to six percentage points a year. These figures compared money-weighted investor returns with time-weighted index returns, that is, the two quantities that diverge in the example above even without any mistake. DALBAR has adjusted its methodology over the years, and today's values are of the same order of magnitude as Morningstar's. The old four to six points continue to be circulated all the same, because they justify an advisory fee.

bloecke.titel: Measurements of the return gap compared

bloecke.md:
In 2025 the gap for equities, at 0.72 percentage points, was the third smallest since 1985. For bonds, by contrast, it was very large at 4.89 points. Investors earned 2.41%, the Bloomberg Aggregate 7.30%. Total outflows reached 6.91% of assets, with a record month in July 2025 (2.30%). The gap is therefore not a fixed human characteristic. It results from the combination of product, market phase and the nerve of the investors concerned.

## The gap and volatility

Morningstar also sorts the funds by their volatility. This produces the most revealing series of figures in the entire study.

bloecke.titel: Return gap by fund category, decade to the end of 2025
bloecke.unter: The less a fund fluctuates, the smaller the gap; in the broad US large blend segment it disappears entirely.

bloecke.md: For crypto ETFs, the gap between January 2024 and December 2025 was around 14 percentage points a year. The investor return was about 22%, the fund return about 36%. The products themselves performed well, but investors got in too late and out too early. The more exciting a fund is, the more certain it is that investors pay for this excitement, through their own timing of purchases and sales and not through the fee.

Behind this lies a simple and therefore stable relationship. Fund inflows follow past returns. After two strong years a fund is at the top of the rankings, attracts money and soon afterwards has more unitholders than ever before, shortly before returns normalise again. A low-volatility fund does not see such strong inflows and outflows, because it is never at the top of the rankings. The gap thus depends less on the intelligence of investors than on how strongly a product tempts people to buy and sell.

## The cost of getting out in Germany

All the figures mentioned come from the USA, where switching funds within retirement accounts is possible free of tax. In a German private portfolio, the same impulsive exit is more expensive.

An accumulating world ETF stands at €100,000; it was bought for €50,000. The market falls by 30%, the portfolio value drops to €70,000, and €20,000 of the book gain remains. At this point the investor sells.

Of the €20,000 gain, after the 30% [[Partial exemption (Teilfreistellung)|partial exemption (Teilfreistellung)]] for equity funds (Section 20(1) InvStG, Investment Tax Act), €14,000 remains taxable, so €13,000 after deducting the [[Saver's allowance (Sparer-Pauschbetrag)|saver's allowance (Sparer-Pauschbetrag)]] of €1,000 (Section 20(9) EStG, Income Tax Act). On this, 26.375% [[Flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer)|flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer)]] including solidarity surcharge is due (Section 32d(1) EStG), which comes to €3,429. The settlement account then holds €66,571.

The market then recovers by 40%. The investor only dares to get back in when the price is 10% above their selling price.

- Holding on: 70,000 × 1.40 = €98,000
- Getting out and coming back: 66,571 × 1.40 / 1.10 = €84,727

The difference of €13,273 is overstated, however, because the returning investor now has a higher cost basis and will pay less tax later. If a notional final sale is calculated for both portfolios (without the allowance being applied again), the result is €89,138 for holding on and €81,375 after coming back. What remains as the price of this one sell decision is around €7,760.

bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation before deferred tax; the flat-rate withholding tax paid is missing together with the return it would have earned, and the missed re-entry costs almost twice as much.

bloecke.md: In a partial sale under stress, the FIFO principle means that the units bought first are mandatorily deemed to have been sold (Section 20(4) sentence 7 EStG). In a savings plan portfolio, these are the units with the highest book gain. The distress sale therefore triggers the highest tax precisely on the units that have been in the portfolio longest.

## Measures against the gap

Education hardly helps. Using organ donation as an example, Johnson and Goldstein showed in 2003 that the default setting achieves much more than knowledge. In the German opt-in system consent was 12%, in the Austrian opt-out system 99.98%. Applied to investing, this means that a decision that has been made once and then automated does not have to be defended every month against your own mood.

The second lever is the evaluation frequency. Benartzi and Thaler showed in 1995 that the combination of loss aversion and short evaluation periods explains why people shy away from shares so strongly. A portfolio app with daily performance and push notifications creates artificially short periods. Looking at your portfolio less often is therefore the cheapest measure available.

- A savings plan with a fixed date is executed on the same day every month, regardless of the news. At many German brokers, executing ETF savings plans is free of charge or limited to a few cents.
- Rebalancing is done by calendar or by range, laid down in writing and not by gut feeling.
- Price push notifications are switched off, and checking the portfolio is set for a fixed date each quarter.
- A **trading budget** limits transactions outside the savings plan, for example to at most four a year. Any further transactions must be justified in writing beforehand.

All you need are two columns listing every payment in and out with its date (contributions negative) and, last of all, today's portfolio value as a positive amount. In Excel or LibreOffice, `=XIRR(values, dates)` returns the money-weighted return per year. Comparing it with the fund's time-weighted return from the factsheet gives your personal gap.

Two limitations apply. With an ongoing savings plan, the result contains the arithmetical part from the example above and is therefore not a verdict on behaviour. In addition, the advance lump sum (Vorabpauschale, Section 18 InvStG) appears as a small payment that increases the cost basis; for the order of magnitude it is negligible.

The behaviour gap is real, but smaller than the figure used in advertising, and it is largest for highly volatile products. The most reliable way to push it down to zero is a boring fund with an automatic savings plan, and not self-control.

mitnehmen: Fund return and investor return measure different things, because one chains periods together and the other weights by money; the difference between them is called the behaviour gap.
Morningstar puts it at 1.2 percentage points a year for the decade to the end of 2025, whereas DALBAR's old values of four to six points are a result of the earlier methodology.
Part of every gap arises without any mistake, solely from a growing portfolio and fluctuating returns; the direction is established, the exact size is open.
The gap grows with volatility, from zero for US large blend equity funds through 2.1 points for the most volatile fifth of funds to around 14 points for crypto ETFs.
In Germany, getting out also costs flat-rate withholding tax, and in the example, after accounting for the deferred tax, a loss of around €7,760 remains from a single sell decision.

begriffe.text: An investor's money-weighted return, calculated as the internal rate of return of all payments in and out, including the final value. It shows what was earned on the money invested, and not how the fund performed.

Annual Morningstar study that compares the fund return and investor return of the same funds over ten years. According to the 2026 edition, they were 9.9% and 8.7% a year in the decade to the end of 2025.

Quantitative Analysis of Investor Behavior, DALBAR's annual report on the return gap of US fund investors, published since 1994 with data from 1985. The four to six percentage points reported in the past were based on a methodology that has since been adjusted.
The interest rate at which the present value of all payments of an investment is zero. It can be calculated in spreadsheets with XIRR and is the basis of every investor return.
